commonProblems.h2: Iveco Stralis Engine Problems - What It Costs to Fix & When Replacement Makes Sense
commonProblems.h3: The Iveco Stralis range-spanning Cursor 8, 9, 10, 11, and 13 engines from 2002 through to 2021-is broadly durable, but no heavy-duty commercial engine is immune to age, mileage, and duty-cycle fatigue. The most common replacement drivers on the Stralis are EGR cooler failures, VGT turbocharger wear, injector faults, and ECM 99 turbo pressure-related issues. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EngineMarket includes upgraded internal components designed to address the original failure point-plus a minimum 12-month unlimited mileage warranty. Below, we break down the real costs of fixing each common fault, and when replacement is the smarter financial decision for your Stralis.

problems.h4: Stralis EGR Cooler Failure - Why Cursor 8, 9 & 13 Engines Suffer Coolant Leaks
problems.affectedModels: Iveco Stralis (2007-2017), Cursor 8 (7.9L), Cursor 9 (8.7L), Cursor 13 (12.9L) - particularly Euro IV and Euro V variants including Hi-Way, Active Space, and Active Time
problems.rootCause: Internal cracking or seal failure within the EGR cooler core allows coolant to leak into the intake manifold. This is often linked to condensation and soot accumulation under sustained low-load or stop-start operating conditions, as noted in IVECO Service Bulletin SB-08-045.
problems.recommendation: If you catch EGR cooler failure early-white exhaust smoke, coolant loss without visible leaks-replacing just the cooler is cost-effective. However, if you've been running with a failed cooler for any length of time, coolant contamination often damages bearings and cylinder liners. On a Stralis with over 400,000 miles, we recommend full replacement with an upgraded unit to avoid repeat failure.
problems.cta: Compare rebuilt Cursor 8, 9 & 13 engine prices for your Stralis

problems.h4: Stralis Turbocharger / VGT Failure - Why Cursor 10 & 13 Engines Lose Power & Trigger ECM 99
problems.affectedModels: Iveco Stralis (2004-2016), Cursor 10 (10.3L), Cursor 13 (12.9L), particularly Euro 4 and Euro 5 variants
problems.rootCause: Variable Geometry Turbo (VGT) mechanism seizes or wears, causing turbo underspeed detection (EDC 2F) and ECM 99 turbo pressure faults. The VGT actuator solenoid, located on the thermostat housing, becomes contaminated with soot and carbon, preventing proper vane movement.
problems.recommendation: ECM 99 is often misdiagnosed. We recommend having a specialist perform a proper turbocharger diagnostic test before replacing anything. If the fault is purely electrical/sensor-related (around £30 for the sensor), the minor fix is excellent value. However, if the VGT mechanism is seized or the turbo has mechanical internal damage, full turbo replacement is the only reliable solution. Full engine replacement is rarely required for turbo failure alone, unless catastrophic failure has occurred.
problems.cta: Compare Stralis turbocharger replacement quotes from UK specialists

problems.group: Stralis Injector & High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure
problems.h4: Stralis Injector & High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure - Why Cursor Engines Suffer Starting & Power Issues
problems.rootCause: Bosch CP3 high-pressure fuel pump wear or injector solenoid failure. Piezoelectric injectors fitted to later Euro 5 and Euro 6 engines are particularly vulnerable and are often irreparable, as the manufacturer does not supply spare parts for 100% functional reconditioning. Injector wiring harness damage on the chassis frame (particularly near the cab right side or engine cushion) is also a known weak point.
problems.recommendation: Injector and pump failures rarely justify full engine replacement on their own. If caught early, replacing individual injectors or the high-pressure pump is the right move. However, if a failed injector has caused cylinder wash-leading to bore scoring and loss of compression-the engine is effectively written off. Always have a specialist perform a compression test and fuel system analysis before committing to repairs.
problems.cta: Compare Stralis injector and fuel system repair costs

problems.group: Stralis Timing Chain & Camshaft Sensor Issues
problems.h4: Stralis Timing Chain & Camshaft Sensor Issues - Why Cursor 8, 10 & 13 Engines Fail to Start or Lose Power Intermittently
problems.rootCause: Gear-driven timing systems on Cursor engines are generally robust, but camshaft position sensors can fail or fall out of range, causing intermittent starting issues and power loss. Timing chain stretch can also occur on higher-mileage units, leading to synchronisation errors between crankshaft and camshaft sensors.
problems.recommendation: Sensor failure is relatively cheap to fix and should always be the first diagnostic step. However, if your Stralis has over 300,000 miles and is showing intermittent starting or power loss, we recommend a specialist timing inspection before replacing sensors. If timing chain or gear wear is confirmed, the major repair is worthwhile on a well-maintained truck. Full engine replacement is only necessary if the timing has failed catastrophically.
problems.cta: Get a Stralis timing system inspection quote from a specialist

problems.h4: Stralis High Oil Consumption - Why Cursor 10 & 13 Engines Burn Oil & Lose Compression
problems.affectedModels: Iveco Stralis (2004-2013), Cursor 10 (10.3L), Cursor 13 (12.9L), Euro 3, Euro 4 and Euro 5 variants
problems.rootCause: Piston ring wear or sticking, leading to oil passing into the combustion chamber. Some Cursor 10 Euro 5 and Euro 5 EEV engines produced between 2011-2013 have documented piston ring wear issues from around 200,000-250,000 km. High oil consumption is a strong indicator that a full engine overhaul or replacement is approaching.
problems.recommendation: High oil consumption on a Stralis is almost always a sign that the engine is nearing the end of its serviceable life. An in-frame piston ring replacement can extend life by 200,000+ miles if caught early and if bores are still within tolerance. However, if oil consumption is severe (over 1 litre per 1,000 miles) or if the truck has over 500,000 miles, full engine replacement with a rebuilt unit is almost always better value than repeated patch repairs.
problems.cta: Compare Stralis engine rebuild vs replacement costs

problems.h4: Stralis ECM 99 Turbo Pressure Fault - The Infamous Stralis Derate & Limp Mode Issue
problems.rootCause: ECM 99 is a turbocharger control pressure monitoring fault. The ECU detects boost pressure that is too high or too low, triggering derate or full stop. The fault often points to the VGT actuator, boost pressure sensor, or a clogged air filter.
problems.recommendation: ECM 99 is one of the most frustrating faults on a Stralis because it can be caused by something as simple as a clogged air filter or as serious as a seized VGT. Start with the cheap fixes-air filter, boost sensor inspection, cleaning the VGT actuator solenoid. If these don't resolve the issue, have a specialist perform a full turbocharger diagnostic test. A new turbo is expensive, but on a Stralis with under 400,000 miles, it's still better value than replacing the entire engine.
problems.cta: Get an ECM 99 diagnostic quote for your Stralis

finalCta.h4: Don't Let Engine Failure Write Off Your Iveco Stralis
finalCta.paragraph: Whether it's a failed EGR cooler, a seized VGT turbo, worn injectors, or the dreaded ECM 99 fault, engine problems on a Stralis don't have to mean the end of the road. faq.h2: Iveco Stralis Engine Replacement - Frequently Asked Questions

items.question: How much does it cost to replace an Iveco Stralis engine in the UK?
items.answer: Expect to pay between £4,000 and £20,000 for a full Iveco Stralis engine rebuild or replacement, depending on the Cursor engine code and whether you choose a used, reconditioned, or new unit.
items.cta: Compare Iveco Stralis engine replacement quotes from UK specialists - get your free estimate today

items.question: How long does an Iveco Stralis Cursor engine last?
items.answer: Cursor family engines (Cursor 9, 10, 11, and 13) are designed for a service life of around 1 million kilometres (over 620,000 miles) with proper maintenance.
items.cta: Find a reconditioned Iveco Stralis engine with a minimum 12‑month warranty

items.question: What are the most common Iveco Stralis engine problems?
items.answer: The most frequently reported issues on Stralis engines are EGR cooler failure (leading to coolant loss), turbocharger/actuator faults (triggering ECM 99 codes), injector failures, and timing chain/tensioner wear.
items.cta: Get a diagnostic quote for your Stralis engine problem from our specialist network

items.question: Which Iveco Stralis engine is the most reliable?
items.answer: The Cursor 10 (10.3-litre) is widely considered the most robust Stralis engine, particularly Euro 3 and Euro 4 variants, with fewer emissions-related failures than later Euro 5 and Euro 6 units.
items.cta: Compare Stralis engine options and prices - find the right engine for your truck

items.question: Is it worth rebuilding my Stralis engine or should I replace it?
items.answer: Rebuilding is usually worthwhile if the rest of the truck is in good condition - especially for Cursor 10 and 13 engines - with savings of up to 30% compared to a new replacement.
items.cta: Get a Stralis engine rebuild vs replacement quote - compare both options

items.question: What engines fit my Iveco Stralis - and how do I find the engine code?
items.answer: Only Cursor family engines (Cursor 8, 9, 10, 11, 13) fit the Stralis - compatibility depends on year, Euro standard, and chassis variant. The engine code is stamped on a metal plate at the rear of the cylinder head, near the turbocharger.
items.cta: Enter your Stralis engine code and get matched to compatible replacement engines

items.question: What does the ECM 99 fault code mean on my Stralis?
items.answer: ECM 99 indicates a turbocharger pressure fault - either too high or too low. It is one of the most common Stralis fault codes and usually points to a faulty VGT actuator, stuck turbo vanes, or a boost pressure sensor issue.
items.cta: Get ECM 99 diagnosed and fixed - find a Stralis engine specialist near you

items.question: Should I choose a used or reconditioned Stralis engine?
items.answer: Choose reconditioned if you want warranty-backed reliability (12-24 months) and peace of mind. Choose used if you're on a tight budget - but verify test history and inspect the engine thoroughly before fitting.
items.cta: Compare used and reconditioned Stralis engine prices side by side

items.question: How long does it take to fit a replacement Stralis engine?
items.answer: A typical Stralis engine supply and fit takes 3-5 working days, depending on the workshop's workload, the engine code, and whether any additional parts (turbo, injectors, cooling system) need replacing at the same time.
items.cta: Get a Stralis engine supply and fit quote with a confirmed turnaround time

items.question: What warranty comes with a replacement Stralis engine?
items.answer: All engines supplied through EnginesMarket carry a minimum 12‑month unlimited mileage warranty - with 24‑month/500,000km options available from some specialist suppliers.
